cues.text: The ancient Greeks did not have just one god.
They had many.
The most important gods were called the Olympians.
People believed they lived on Mount Olympus.
At 2,917 metres, it is the highest mountain in Greece, and its top is often hidden in clouds.
So it seemed the right home for gods.
People could see the mountain, but they could not see what happened at the top.
The Greek gods looked like people and acted like people.
They fell in love, became angry and jealous, and argued with each other.
They were a family, with parents, brothers, sisters and children.
But there was one big difference: they were immortal.
They never died.
A Greek god was like a person with enormous power and no end.
Because the gods had human feelings, the Greeks believed they could please them with gifts.
The most important gift was a sacrifice: people killed an animal on an altar, a stone table for gifts.
The altar stood outside, in front of the temple.
The temple was the house of the god, and a statue of the god stood inside.
In a sacrifice, people burned the bones and fat for the god.
Then they cooked the meat and ate it together.
Meat was expensive, so many Greeks rarely ate it except at festivals for the gods.
The biggest festival was at Olympia, a holy place of Zeus.
About 2,800 years ago, the Greeks started the Olympic Games there.
They held them every four years to please Zeus.
The Games were sport, but they were also religion.
During the Games, 100 bulls were killed for Zeus.
Then the crowd shared a huge meal of meat, bread, olives and wine.
Zeus was the king of the gods.
He ruled the sky and the weather.
He gathered the clouds, sent the rain, and threw thunderbolts when he was angry.
A thunderbolt is lightning used as a weapon.
In paintings and statues, he usually holds a thunderbolt in his hand.
His most famous story explains how he became king.
His father, Cronus, ruled the world before him.
Cronus was afraid that one of his children would take his power.
So every time his wife Rhea had a baby, he swallowed it whole.
When Zeus was born, Rhea had a plan.
She wrapped a stone in baby clothes and gave it to Cronus.
He swallowed the stone without noticing.
The real baby grew up in secret on the island of Crete.
When Zeus was an adult, he forced his father to throw up his brothers and sisters, still alive.
Together they fought Cronus and won.
The story shows the character of Zeus: clever, strong and ready to fight for power.
Why did the Greeks need Zeus?
First, most of them were farmers, and their crops needed rain.
Second, Zeus kept order among gods and people, and he protected guests.
When a stranger knocked on your door, Zeus wanted you to give them food and a bed.
Travelling was slow and dangerous, so a traveller often depended on the kindness of strangers.
Zeus turned that kindness into a duty.
After their victory, Zeus and his two brothers drew lots to share the world.
Drawing lots is choosing by chance, like picking a paper from a box.
Zeus got the sky, Hades got the underworld, the land of the dead, and Poseidon got the sea.
Poseidon carries a trident, a big fork with three points.
People used tools like this to catch fish.
Poseidon did not rule only the water.
The Greeks also called him the Earth-shaker.
They believed he caused earthquakes by hitting the ground with his trident.
Greece has many earthquakes, and it has sea on three sides and thousands of islands.
Sailors gave gifts to Poseidon and asked him to protect them.
For them, a calm sea meant life, and a storm meant death.
At Sounion, on a cliff south-east of Athens, his temple still stands above the water.
Ships on their way to Athens could see it.
His most famous story shows that Poseidon did not easily forgive anyone who hurt his family.
In the Odyssey, a famous Greek poem, the hero Odysseus is going home after a long war.
On an island, a giant with one eye traps him and his men in a cave.
The giant, Polyphemus, begins to eat them.
Odysseus escapes by blinding the giant.
But Polyphemus is the son of Poseidon.
The angry god sends storms, and Odysseus wanders the sea for ten years before he gets home.
For the Greeks, the message was clear.
The sea is powerful, it does not forget, and you must respect it.
Athena was a daughter of Zeus and his favourite child.
She was the goddess of wisdom, but also of war and of crafts like making cloth.
This seems strange, but there is a reason.
In war, Athena was the goddess of clever plans, not of anger or strength.
Plans, not anger, win a war.
Her bird was the owl, and the Greeks connected owls with wisdom.
Her most famous story is a contest for a city.
Athena and Poseidon both wanted to protect the same city in Greece.
So each god gave the people a gift.
Poseidon hit a rock with his trident, and water came out.
But it was salt water, like the sea.
The people could not drink it or use it on their fields.
Athena made an olive tree grow.
The people chose her gift, and the city took her name: Athens.
Why was a tree better than water?
Olives were food, and olive oil was used for cooking, for lamps at night and for cleaning the body.
Olive trees also grow well in dry Greek land and live for hundreds of years.
Olive oil was so valuable that winners at the festival of Athena received large jars of it as prizes.
Her gift was not exciting, but it was useful for a very long time.
That is exactly her character: she thinks about the future.
The people of Athens thanked her with the Parthenon, a great temple.
It stands on the Acropolis, the hill of rock above the city.
Inside stood a statue of Athena, more than 12 metres tall, made of gold and ivory.
Stone figures high on one end of the building told the story of the contest with Poseidon.
Demeter was the goddess of the harvest, the time when farmers collect their crops.
She helped the plants in the fields grow.
From these plants came bread, the most important food in Greece.
Without Demeter, the Greeks believed, there would be nothing to eat.
Her story is also the Greek explanation for the seasons.
Demeter had a daughter, Persephone, whom she loved more than anything.
One day, Persephone was picking flowers.
Suddenly Hades, the god of the underworld, came up from the ground.
He carried her away to his dark kingdom to be his wife.
Demeter searched the whole earth for her daughter.
She was so sad that she stopped looking after the plants.
Nothing grew, and people began to die of hunger.
Finally, Zeus told Hades to send Persephone back.
But before she left, Hades gave her a pomegranate seed, and she ate it.
A pomegranate is a round red fruit full of small seeds.
Hades knew that food from the underworld would tie her to his kingdom.
So Persephone had to spend one third of every year with Hades, and the rest with her mother.
This, the Greeks said, is why winter comes.
When Persephone is in the underworld, Demeter is sad, and the fields are empty.
When her daughter returns, Demeter is happy, and spring arrives with flowers and young plants.
The myth gave farmers a reason for the hard months and a promise that life always comes back.
The temples are ruins now, but the gods are still part of daily life.
The clearest example is the Olympic flame.
A few months before every Olympic Games, there is a ceremony at Olympia.
It takes place in front of the Temple of Hera.
Hera was the wife of Zeus.
An actress is dressed like a woman from an ancient temple.
She holds a torch above a curved mirror.
A torch is a stick for carrying fire.
The mirror collects sunlight into one very hot point.
This heat lights the torch.
Then many runners carry the fire on its way to the city that hosts the Games.
The ceremony is modern, but it happens where the ancient Games for Zeus took place.
So the modern Games begin with fire from the holy place of the old Games.
The gods are also in shops.
In 1971, a sports company in the United States chose the name Nike for its new shoes.
Nike was the goddess of victory.
She was a less important goddess, often with wings.
The giant statue of Athena in the Parthenon held a small Nike in her right hand.
For a sports company, the name was perfect: every athlete wants to win.
Finally, the gods are in people's pockets.
The Greek one-euro coin shows an owl, the bird of Athena.
Its design copies a coin that Athens used about 2,500 years ago.
When people in Greece buy a coffee today, they may pay with the same owl as ancient Athens.
